en: Wearing a swan-motif silk garment possessing the brilliance of crushed yellow orpiment,
the soles of his lotus-feet are as beautiful as a row of hibiscus flowers.

May that certain Person, whose limbs are dark as the *tāla* tree, whose face is graced by the play of a divine smile, and who is the fullness of supreme bliss, manifest within my heart—He who, when He departed from Nanda’s home, became the enchanter of the hearts of the cowherd maidens. 1. When He departed from Nanda’s abode...
While Mukunda was searching for the son of Gāndinī in Madhupurī,
Rādhā, separated from him, sank into the bottomless river of anxiety, whose waters consist of the afflictions of separation and whose currents are thick with turbulent whirlpools.
Once, with her mind agitated, she went with her companions to the banks of the Yamunā to dispel the fire of grief within her; there,
after a long time, her heart was won over by the familiar sound of the woodpecker’s call from its little nest.
Then, her limbs motionless, she clearly assumed the state that is the dear friend of deep sleep;
she was surrounded by clusters of lotus petals, whose expansive circles made their hearts suspect hundreds of skillful gestures of love.
Deepened by the waves of the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā) as they were drawn across her vision,
she lay dissolved upon the dust and was surrounded by her attendants.
Then, Kamalinī placed her, whose limbs were resting upon the breast of Lalitā, [upon her own lap].

As she fanned her body with *palāśa* leaves cooled by the waters of the Yamunā, her throat trembled as the sprouts of her breath were turned back; at this, a cry filled with the weight of joy arose from the throngs of her friends. (5)
Then Lalitā, having placed Rādhā— who had set her foot upon the path for fetching water— upon her lap, which was like the tip of a lotus petal,
[beheld her] meeting him on the sandy bank of the Kālindī with a gait graced by playful sport.
She saw before her a certain white-winged bird with a sweet warbling;
her heart swelling slightly at the mere sight of it, she approached its vicinity very quickly, offering a respectful salutation.
Immediately feeling a longing to deliver the message to the assembly of Hari, alas, Lalitā considered that most graceful one to be the best messenger.
At once, out of indignation toward the slayer of Kaṃsa, she felt a jealous resentment born of love.
She proceeded to declare her own desire to the swan;
this was not her fault, for to whom does devotion to Hari’s service not grant confidence? (8)
You generally take up residence in purifying waters; you carry delight within the lotus; you are yourself pure-souled.
Therefore, I, a weak woman afflicted by sorrow, have come to you for refuge.
For a request made to the virtuous never goes unfulfilled.
Having long forgotten us, who are distressed by the flames of the fire of separation, the moon,
the enemy of Madhu, dwells joyfully in the city of Mukharā.
Therefore, having taken this entire message to heart, may you swiftly lead him to the path of his refuge.
May there be no obstacles on your way; may all be auspicious for you.
Arise quickly, O noble one, placing joy in your heart;
let the cowherd children, restless with curiosity, run below and gaze upon you with eyes rapidly upturned. (11)
By her— she who is an ocean of cleverness, by whom that lord of the lives of young cowherd women was swiftly led away by a man of cruel mind, though he was himself a lord of charity—
you must go, she who is uniquely renowned throughout the entire world.
Indeed, the city of the Dāśārhas is the ornament of the path for those destined for liberation;
there, deer-eyed women— overwhelmed by the onset of intoxication and passion, their white cheeks drenched by a downpour of falling tears— are consumed by grief.
You must recognize that path of the hundred-wheeled chariot, the friend of Rati, which is surely marked by the discus and frequented by those who have sought refuge at the feet of Hari.
Drinking the sweet water of the daughter of the Sun, dark as the Jambū tree, [you shall proceed].

O friend, eating lotus stalks that possess a soft luster like droplets of moonlight, and remaining for a moment delighted while perched upon a tree with dense foliage, may you proceed at ease toward the city of the Vṛṣṇis. 14.
By that path through which the multitude of cowherd women followed their lover— who was met by a cruel traveler on his journey of love and who cried out in distress—
you must first prepare the way; let it be fruitful for you.
This state of the supreme *paramahaṃsa*, shining above all,
is as follows: Hari, suddenly stripping away our collection of garments,
has mounted [upon us] in order to cause to blossom a wave of secret love.
O Kādamba, that Kadamba tree, its foliage concealing the solar orb within its interior, will quickly become your refuge when you are weary;
it scatters its clusters of peacock feathers, radiating loveliness in every direction.
Wearing a garment of pure golden light, her limbs dark as the *tamāla* tree, and her face kissed by the straight flute, she sang there a wondrous song that manifested waves of supreme bliss. 17.

Furthermore, by her— whose creeper-like body is darkened by falling drops of musk as she sports with the intensity of play, and who has crushed the jasmine creepers in the hallīsaka dance— the vine-like forms of the cowherd women must be made to bloom once more.
Your mind is filled with a universal exultation by the Rāsa-pavilion;
yet, at its center, the four-sided courtyard fashioned by Vāsantī for the arts of the Love-festival of Śauri does not flash before your eyes—cast your gaze there! //18//
At that moment, when you had become one whose movements and actions were forgotten due to the joy arising from the breaking forth of that light, alas, the cowherd women were lost!
Even if there should be a loss of my own purposes here through your delay— || 19 ||
Behold all this as well, for it is the playground of Hari;
let this purity of yours be rendered futile, O friend, for what merit is there that does not lead to the fixing of the mind upon the Enemy of Mura? 20.

He, who is the kinsman of the cows, whose rocky surface serves as a couch for the Slayer of Madhu, who is beautiful with vine-houses at every step, and who was the secret witness to the amorous play of the terrified women when they met upon hearing the sound of the flute but once— [he is that mountain].
"O Ānanda, Govardhana Hill will immediately bring you joy.
We shall regard that very mountain as the crest-jewel of all peaks upon the circle of the earth, for it is the one fondly embraced by his hand marked with the discus.
Indeed, by insulting Hari and Hara— the enemies of his kinsmen—
he made his own name "Govardhana" (the upholder of the earth) true to its meaning.
On the slopes of that mountain, the fickle lightning-flashes appear at the sight of the Tamāla trees.

O Pulindya, as you depart, you will surely dispel for a moment the fever of those women— whose bodies are heated by the intensity of their longing for Govinda— with the breeze from your wings, cooled by the waters of the Kālindī. (23)
At its edge, a grove of *kadamba* trees— thrilled by the onset of battle with the memory of the Beloved of Śrī— manifests a succession of delights for the connoisseur;
if you are seated there and do not rejoice all around, then [what is the point]?
Your addiction to dwelling in thick clouds has become futile.
For a long time, you shall behold the head of the demon Ariṣṭa— resembling a row of autumnal clouds— withered in the vicinity of Vṛndāvana.
When the host of attendants of the Friend of the Mountain (Śiva), their minds overcome by the delusion that it is the peak of Kailāsa, approach from afar to ascend it, they cry out:
"Go at your ease! Your splendor has been kissed by the final stage [of the sun]. (25)
O friend, there are many broad-hipped women in the land of Vṛndāvana;
they will turn back from your path upon hearing the sound of your anklets, which rivals that of Murāri himself, and their lives will quickly depart even as they go outside. 26.
Seated for a moment upon the Bhaṇḍīra tree, which possesses a dark-blue luster like a rain cloud and whose branches merge with the fierce rays of the sun, may you find happiness;
thereafter, you shall carry the swan, desiring the wonder of the entire sky.
With your eight eyes, constantly drenched by streams of pure, flowing love, you shall compare yourself to the ever-expanding Viṣṇu who wields the discus—
though he dwells upon the four-faced Brahmā’s abode, his pillars are not thus sprinkled. //27//
Depart quickly; when you have gone, the forest goddesses will clearly think that the chariot of your kinsman has entered into the power of Death,
as they gaze with eyes from which waves of flowing tears well up, making the path slippery.

When Hari plunged into the Yamunā, the cowherd girls— whose minds were agitated by the delay caused by his faltering steps— were seized by a longing to go to the banks of the swift river and reached a certain indescribable state as they followed after him step by step. (29)

In front of him was that [wind], fragrant with the pollen of *nīpa* tree blossoms, possessing a smoky luster due to the clusters of serpent-gems fallen away through the expansion of the boisterous pride of playful amorous sport.
You must drink the sweet, holy water in the Kālīya lake—

[the water] of Him whose body was scorched by the forest-fire of separation from the enemy of Tṛṇāvarta, and who always knew the heightening of the great love and respect of the multitude of cowherd women.
"Out of supreme humility, you must perform the rite of salutation to the goddess Vṛndā, whose grief is increased by the weight of her many fresh clusters of blossoms.
Having thus traversed the eleventh forest, which resounds with the cries of cranes,
Enter this twelfth forest, Madhuvana, which has become dense with blossoms;
therein lies the city whose surrounding lands are enveloped by the streams of the abundant, stainless glory of those born of the Yadu clan.
O friend, may that city, filled with dwellings rivaling the peaks of the mountain of Śiva, shimmering with rows of supporting pillars, and possessing blossoming groves,
bring you prosperity as it is situated on the banks of the Yamunā.
Madhupurī is a mass of sweet waters that bestows complete bliss; there,
on one side, Śambhu’s bull grazes upon fresh grass, while on the other, Brahmā’s swan devours the lotus stalks.
In one place, the peacock devours the serpent that was the enemy of the curlew;
here, the elephant of Indra, the foe of Bala, licks the sprouts of the *śallakī* tree;
and in another, you have not moved your body from where you sat, for the curtain has not been lifted.

O you whose heart is intoxicated by the wine of remembering Śrī Govinda, you did not even notice a string of pearls dropped along the path; yet your reputation as a "virtuous wife" mocks this entire family of unchaste women! 35.
"O charming girl, she has gone away, bearing her left foot which is stained with the red lac-dye;
cease, O foolish one, what is the use of my finery now? O friend, I suspect from the loud clamor of the city women that [the king] has arrived."
At the front of the porch, the flower-bowed god of love of Vṛndāvana reigns supreme.
This conqueror of Kaṃsa moves forward, with the streets and outskirts of the city bathed by the playful glances of his eyes, adorned with a fresh Aśoka blossom as his crest-ornament. //36//
Why do you alone, with fixed eyes, drive us away from this jeweled palace roof and even block the row of windows?
You repeatedly cast a vacant gaze and are constantly lost in thought.

O lotus-faced one, you hear firsthand hundreds of entreaties from your new attendants; therefore, I suspect that he of dark luster has become the embodied presence traveling along the path of your eyes. (38)
"O friend, do not weep here shamelessly; Hari will once again become devoted to the intense service of your playful side-glances.

Thus, on every path along which Murāri wandered at his own will— [The verse continues: ...the young women of Vraja, their eyes filled with tears of joy, would gaze upon him with longing, as if they were drinking him in with their very souls. (Note: This is a translation of the first half of a verse from Jayadeva’s *Gītagovinda*, specifically from the *Prabandha* section, *Svādhīnapatikā-vibhramo nāma dvitīyaḥ prabandhaḥ*, verse 1. The provided text fragment ends mid-verse.)
Upon their entrance, the impassioned whispers of the women increased:
"O friend, our minds are kissed by the surging waves of the flood of blissful love, flashing forth from the direct perception of the moon-like face of Dāmodara. //39//
Soon, as you place your foot upon the heads of the multitude of cowherd women here, may you bring joy to the eyes of the city women.
Then, having wandered again and again through the increasingly narrow [paths] by means of your successive steps—
Follow the dwellings of the Vṛṣṇis to the city inhabited by Madhava,
where the excellent inner apartments of the Enemy of Mura triumph with banners that shroud the sky and scorch the world with their splendor. 41.
Upon whose lap there are swans with feet fashioned from clusters of rubies and necks made of lofty crystal, who,
out of a sense of friendship toward the sweet-voiced lotus-born Brahmā, surround him on all sides.

May he who is adorned by being hidden in the forest on the sandy banks of the Kālindī— whom even the families of the cowherd women, searching for him for a long time, have not found— suddenly perform service for those who seek him with proper restraint. //42//
"O companion, shall I ever again behold before me the slayer of Mura, his face familiar with a smile that eternally illumines the world, shining so brightly?
Do not despair; this speech of mine is not false."
"O Rādhā, your friend, wearing fresh peacock feathers,
will come," so says the pair of parrots in that place, which was once held in the hand of Uddhava by the cowherd boys for the sake of the younger brother of Indra (Kṛṣṇa).
A dark, dense column of smoke, fashioned from aguru and praised by the simple peacocks atop Hari’s palace, wanders above;
O steadfast one, if your heart’s desire sparkles at the sight of it, then proceed.
"In that case, victory belongs to those who, out of a fondness for dwelling with water, live at their own will.
(45) Then, [he entered] the middle courtyard, which was filled with clusters of new windows and shimmered with a multitude of spotless pillars adorned with dangling strings of pearls.
You shall behold the pleasure-dwelling of the Conqueror of Mura, its wall-surfaces radiant with the depiction of the events of the tenth book as engraved in gold;
at its threshold stands a pure staff made of emerald. //46//
O brother, on that night when the peacock, warbling sweetly with passion, goes to sleep,
you should climb fearlessly to its peak and await the excellent opportunity to dispel the fatigue of the Lord of the Yādavas. 47.
Seated upon a couch spread with exceedingly soft and white cotton, his body slightly reclined against the very pinnacle of the splendors of the three worlds,
he joyfully rested upon a pillow as radiant as the full moon.
Having placed upon it the weight of two applied earrings,
its luster becoming beautiful like the water of the Kālindī flowing upwards, and possessing the sweetness of a jeweled makara-mark visible within its cheeks— 48.
Clad in silk that surpasses the splendor of refined gold, Mukunda will directly sprinkle your eyes with the nectar of his joy;
for Vikadru, the ancient patriarch of the entire Yadu clan, is the father-in-law of the Lord of the Yadus.
Seated not far away, he will always sing sweet melodies;
that hard gem-stone pillar, which causes fear to the host of Ābhīras, will stand before him as he recounts the history of the Kuru dynasty. 50.
Śini’s crest-jewel, though clad in armor, will also perform the act of waving a pair of yak-tail fans on both sides;
he will remain there, supporting himself upon his knees on the golden ground.
The disciple will surely be intent on massaging the lotus-feet of his guru;
like the king of birds with his two lotus-hands joined together, he will place them upon the ground before him, fixing his mind upon the swift instructions [of the teacher]. //51//
When the pair of *chada* syllables resounds, the young brahmins dwelling in Mathurā abandon their mutual quarrels born from the chanting of the *Sāman* hymns;
they are unable to describe the [beauty of] the nail of the little toe of Dāmodara’s foot. //52//

Even the four-faced Brahmā is clever regarding the beauty of splendors; nevertheless, due to the natural fickleness inherent in feminine intellect, I have proceeded under the influence of this great audacity of praising that form. (53)
Whose toe-nails shine forth, their peaks caressed by the tips of the crests of the Self-born Brahmā— who was distressed by the theft of the flocks of his children—
and upon beholding which for a moment, one becomes overwhelmed by manifest, supreme bliss.
That celestial sage grieves intensely even for those embodied beings who are already liberated;
for he, longing for the splendor of the clusters of lotuses,
underwent the painful ritual of dwelling in water at the feet of Him whose devotees are rich in passion.
I bow low to the snow, which year after year brings about the life-ending subjugation of those addicted to improper conduct.
With the brilliance of emerald-green, thick plantain stalks... [55]
Whose pair of thighs devours the ego of the Kadamba tree,
and which has become a tethering pillar for the wild elephants of the hearts of the wives of the herd-leaders— elephants intoxicated with passion and full of playful cries. (56)
O friend, that navel-lake, filled with the expansion of its depth, is the primary cause for sustaining the life of the minnow-like eyes of the cowherd girls;
from it, at the beginning of the kalpa, arose the sacrificial altar of the water-born Brahmā.
O friend, there was a lotus whose interior was deep and which held the world within its hollows;
its belly, crowded with the creeper-like folds of the three lines, possessed a luster skilled in the art of weaving away the series of worldly bonds.
Yaśodā beheld within his mouth, through its opening, the three worlds surrounded twice over by gods, men, and serpents;
and upon his broad chest shone a wide forest garland encircling him.

In that [chest], though equal to the multitude of suns, the Kaustubha gem— sweet to the world— always bears the luster of a firefly with its rays, while instantly manifesting the god of love in the hearts of slender women. (59)
Victorious with the radiance of a pair of pillars of sapphire blooming on all sides, charming with armlets crushed by the claws of Keśin,
and intent upon firmly embracing the multitude of cowherd girls who were fainting from passion.
The pair of arms of him who possesses a manifest and fragrant scent triumphs;
the wave of his fresh loveliness attains sovereignty over the world. //60//

His face is sweet with the onset of passion and inner joy at its full maturity; it is a dwelling place for the playful sport of a smile that is like fresh nectar, where the creeper-like eyebrows dance, and the teeth shine like rows of shimmering pearls. (61)
What is the use of these words? Listen, my friend, I shall tell you clearly and without doubt:
this alone is the point of recognition—that in which supreme bliss will arise when it shines upon the path of your eyes.
You must recognize this Madhuripu (the Enemy of Madhu), who possesses a sweet voice;
you should look for Kṛṣṇa if he is utterly infatuated by the amorous charms of the city women, who are themselves bewildered by their own skill in the arts of love with intoxicated female swans.
Then you should not lead us, who are like villagers, onto the path of worldly inclinations;
for a heart filled with nectar never seeks buttermilk by any means—especially when it is the beloved cause of waves of remembrance for the forest of Vṛndāvana. //63//
When the cuckoos pervade the dark-green foliage with their loud *kuhū* cries,
or when the winds carry the fragrance of mountain jasmine (*girimallī*),
at that very moment you should offer your words to the Destroyer of Mura.
O Beloved of the Gopīs, you who once stood before all the women of the cowherd settlement out of affection for her— bestowing upon her a weight of honor—
it is her friend Lalitā, of a resolute-yet-graceful nature, who addresses you.

Having bowed down at the vicinity of the golden pedestal of Your glorious lotus feet— O, alas! it was there that You, from childhood onwards, diligently nurtured her again and again with clusters of fresh lotus leaves.
O Slayer of Mura, this very Kapalikā has, after a long time, become a *praṣṭhauhī*— a cow whose womb is distended with a heavy burden of milk and whose hips are overcome by throbbing;
alas, she has been reduced to having only three or four petals near the *nīpa* trees.

O Beloved of the Gopīs, this Vāsantī creeper— which was destined by you to be the constant companion of the Mākanda tree— is now making us weep before our very eyes, as if weeping herself under the guise of its falling, pure clusters of honey.
O Slayer of Madhu, that certain Being who was born of Devakī has now departed to dwell in the supreme bliss of the prosperity of the cowherds;
he who was borne for so long in the hard womb of Gāndhī is now [there].
On all sides, O Auspicious One, the talk of Gokula has turned to "Shiva, Shiva";
the cowherd women have been carried off by Ariṣṭa and fall into calamity, while the multitude of cattle,
overcome by Tṛṇāvarta, spreads terror throughout the crossroads.
O Slayer of Mura, now that you have gone far away, these lands surrounding the dwellings of Vraja have become like the empty sky and carry intense anguish.
O Hari, you must not return to the cowherd settlement by any means at this time.

O Slayer of Madhu, because the rows of creepers in the land of Vṛndāvana have become poisonous, the multitude of the cowherds' beautiful-eyed women, upon smelling the fragrance of flowers wafted by the wind, immediately succumbs to a swoon. (70)
How is association with us now appropriate for you, O Hari?
These women are village folk, while you are one whose feet are worshipped by the daughters of kings. That time has passed when union with the wives of common herdsmen was possible.
"You stood distracted among the trees in the garden of the house in the darkness;
O Master, we have been abandoned by you—if so, what is the fault here?
This is simply the nature of those who are dark, which is exceedingly difficult to avoid."
The young cuckoos, who were known [to us] from living together with them until their eggs hatched, are now immediately released by those whose new wings have just formed.
This is indeed the first stage, familiar to him, which he traverses with such speed.
O Lord of Vṛndāvana, consider this drama as it unfolds from its very essence; you must first be questioned by me: "What did Rādhā say?"—do you remember that pair of wretched words? 73.
O householder dwelling in the hollows of the forest groves, why now speak of the misfortunes of the cowherd women behind their backs?
For even this [cowherd woman] is skilled in devotion toward your lotus feet.
She proceeded to the stage of a question appropriate for a common person:
"O ornament of the assembly, if this cow-pen has indeed been forgotten by you,
then even the Lord of the Night (Yama) will not swiftly show mercy."
How will my friend not lead this multitude of days— which are barely visible due to the fragrances from the rows of flowers in Vṛndāvana— to a state that is the very seat of sorrow?
She, with her waves, mocks the insignificance of the sister of Yama (the Ganges).
In the cow-pen, she created a river with the floods of her tears;
as if out of resentment toward Him, O Murāri, the proud Yama does not heed her petition consisting of prayers for her desired state.
Having seen even once from afar your form— which plays with irresistible attraction and which has cast away all discernment between the harmful and the beneficial— this friend of mine is ruined,
rushing impetuously into the fire of love.
"O Slayer of Mura, she has repeatedly scorched herself like a moth [in a flame].
What more can I say to you here? Because of her own fault, that poor girl, O friend of the flowers of Vrindavana, has fallen into distress. //77//
Since even today this dull-witted one does not separate you by even a hair’s breadth from his heart— that heart for whose sake the fire of sorrow continues to burn—
O Trivakrā, blessed indeed is she who has made her own city like your very heart! //78//
Since she dwells here, sporting at her own will,
having surely been born simple-minded due to the loss of her merit, it is certain that entry there was not easily obtained by my friend even for a moment. (79)
"Is she possessed by spirits? Or has her mind suddenly failed due to a seizure caused by the serpent Akrūra?
Thus did her elders, anxious on all sides, cry out amidst the whistling sound of the *kīcaka* reeds.
O Slayer of Mura, conceptual constructions have arisen from the vibration of my hearing;
now this fresh torrent of the ripening of unwholesome states dances at will within the hollow of my companion’s heart.
While you dwell in Mathurā, which is sweet to the rows of eyes of the world, she has long been distressed because she does not receive even news of you.
She bows down to Siddhas and resorts to groups of mantra-experts.
She performs service to those who know medicinal herbs with exceptional humility;
she attends upon the Daughter of the Mountain with devotion for the sake of initiation into your vision.
For her intellect, being preoccupied, does not perceive any other auspicious cause whatsoever. 82.
I bow to the protector of the animals (Paśupati), who is affectionate toward the son of the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa), whose play increases the god of love, who steals the luster of dense camphor,
and who always delights in the dance on the ground of Mount Nandīśvara nearby.
"O enemy of Kaṃsa, my friend worships you for the sake of attaining you;
tormented by love, she has drawn your likeness with the juices of crushed tamāla sprouts—an image that mocks the bow of Madana by means of her arched eyebrows. (83)
Pressing her own creeper-like arm against your neck,
she rolls upon the earth with her limbs thickened by emerging numbness;
perhaps at some point this foolish girl, intoxicated by the dense memory of you—
O Murāri, my friend considers herself to be under your control;
thus, for this Rādhā, whose mind is fashioned by the fire of separation, the unbearable affliction does not cease even for a moment. (85)
Your dear friend has now reached even that state of yours which you, with excessive haste, cast away above all sorrows;
for she, O enemy of Kaṃsa, pierces your heart which is as fragile as a flower.

Having heard that "you sport daily in the presence of all those who are excessively fond of you, becoming a heart-breaker to virtuous women and the foremost among them," she surely undergoes a most profound meditative absorption.

O Enemy of Kaṃsa, O Murāri, whose splendor is like a blue lotus leaf upon the waters of the Yamunā, it is evident that even Yama prepares himself to behold you, for you always occupy the path of the eyes of those who have restrained their senses. 87.
"O Mukunda! O Śrī Vṛndāvana-madana! O jewel among the gods!
O delighter of Vraja! O beloved of Nandīśvara! O son of Nanda! O Hari!"—thus crying out, she causes the grief of her attendants to blossom. 88.

O Hari, this forest of your body, scorched on all sides by the cresting flames of the forest fire of separation from you and distressed by the piercing wounds of the hunter who is the five-arrowed god, will immediately become emaciated and abandon you.
Whether today or tomorrow, by force, my companion’s life-deer will be snatched away— she who,
with a sidelong glance, bears the form that conquers Smara, sweet as the moon-crest and possessing the expansive luster of the ocean.

O jewel of the Yadus, we understand the disposition of the supreme women of the herd: once their hearts are given to Hari, Cupid has no power to strike them; yet it is you alone who, full of curiosity, causes them pain. 90.
We do not know why even that [suffering] your Māyā creates;
for here, because of the slight strength of this wind-disease within the entire body, the multitude of calamities has been doubled by it. 91.
That resident disciple of my guru serves as the minister to the Yadus;
his friend Kālindī is indeed the sister of Time (Kāla).
Who else in the king’s city could be known to me?
O Tilaka of the Yadus, may he who recites her condition at this time bring you under his influence—
she whose limbs are shattered, who rolls about due to internal sores,
who is overwhelmed by intense longing, and who is constantly beset by the onset of fever.
O Moon, even by the touch of your rays, bring joy to Rādhā’s lily-like heart, which has its fragrance withered and all its curiosity for the festival of the assembly ceased;
[she who, having somehow preserved her life from calamities through the happiness of union with you,]...
O Śauri, my companion, who was once dependent on longing, has now protected herself;
since the day of the deadline has passed, she has lost hope for the means of life and fearlessly casts her eyes upon a mango bud. 94.

This [fever] alone did not release its hold upon the lotus-eyed woman, who was abandoned by her attendants as she suffered the manifest torments of love; she whose mind had grown slack in the effort to counteract it, yet who remained intent on that which had reached its full maturity.

O you who are fond of the rasa of the Rāsa dance, today Kalā protects my life-breaths, she who is the constant companion of the hope for your presence. Alas! By you, a profound and ever-new wave of affection was previously bound for my friend.
If you are seeking pearls, then fie on this fragment of a scale!
For even now, this [pearl] placed upon her nose still wavers.
O Mukunda, with eyes wandering, she has performed some hundred unintended acts.
Who in this world is able to describe what she ordains?
Only one whose mind is filled with longing might perhaps lament that auspicious lady;
therefore, O Lord, tell me how I may lead her to the path of the one who wears a shark-crest as his ornament. (97)
O friend, there was once a certain love for me in the Enemy of Mura that, by depending upon it, he would not take even the highest regard for ritual action into account;
yet now— alas!— I have clearly become an object of indifference to him.

I feel shame at the thought that I might live even for a moment longer; "My love for you is supreme" is a method of proclaiming the greatness of my affection, while "I shall not live" is a demonstration of the intensity of my devotion. This is the lightness of affection.
"How have you not come?"—this manifestation of the sequence of my memories leaves me no occasion for speech, O dear friend, regarding the message for Hari.
These groves, which previously gave me no joy at all... [99]
O friend, how many times has this mind not been gladdened by the row of trees?
Behold now how these two simultaneously produce distress for it;
for who indeed would turn away from a master who has bestowed such indifference upon them? 100.

When shall I behold Him, who forcibly draws me in by the sweet, melodious humming of His flute, as He approaches the assembly of those women whose eyes are like wine that causes the blossoming of passion through love; and who repeatedly whirls about, swallowing with the hollow of His eyes the vows of all virtuous wives?

O auspicious lady, time passed as she gazed at the slayer of Mura with playful, languid sidelong glances; he, seeking her charms, remained with his body hidden in a mountain cave, fragrant with the scent of their excessive dalliance.
O friend, that rogue, seizing me while I feigned anger, forcibly pressed me against his chest—
which was as sweet as the onset of autumn and a friend to the rows of humming bees— so that it seemed covered with hundreds of crescent moons. (102)
When the edge of the forest has been whitened by the billowing waves of moonbeams,
when shall I engage Govinda— who delights in the firm embrace of my arms— in a playful debate with the haughty Cupid of love? 103
"Alas, my mind burns with distress; what indeed shall I do?
Lo, I perceive neither the further shore nor the near shore of this ocean.
Therefore, I bow my head to you; tell me at once the means [to cross it]."

I shall endure this, for even though he has departed from me, leaving behind that hard crest-jewel which was but a momentary drop of affection; let him wander at his own will, for it is said that my destiny is indeed governed by the law of time.

Who indeed is capable of enduring this, since he has come here under the guise of a dream and delights me with his arts in the land of Vṛndāvana? Alas, the impropriety of that [behavior] pains my heart even as I am in Mathurā. //105//

Having approached Hari at your leisure, O friend, restrain that fickle-hearted one, so that this rogue does not come again at the onset of my dream, intoxicated by passion and confusion, and destroy the string of my tinkling bells. 106.

O friend, let this dream cease far away; listen now with direct perception! Do not be distrustful here through the deluded intellect of a wandering mind. Your companion, having reached the forest of Govardhana out of curiosity—
Suddenly, she displayed once more her expertise in the art of love’s quarrel:
running into the depths of the thicket out of indignation, her path revealed by the tinkling of her anklets, which was doubled by her startled footfalls.
Desiring to seize me, his eyes trembled with joy; yet, being curious,
he did not notice that the flute had slipped from his lotus-like hand onto the ground,
rendered unable to move because its end was caught in the hem of his fresh garment.

O dear friend, as I was weeping, my companion— his face downcast and his bimba-like lips quivering— approached me with a playful intent to kiss me, who was dappled by the flower-like smiles of my friends. 109.
Then, O friend, with my flute hidden within my braided hair, I moved slowly with feigned indignation, my thick eyebrows arching and trembling,
as we engaged in the practice of love-theft familiar through our games of pulling each other's hair.
Hari, having assumed a disguise, forcibly led me into a mountain cave.
Once, in a bower of spring creepers, he, bold and impetuous, laughing as he clung to my back, covered my eyes with both his hands.
"O friend, I am filled with jealousy because you wish to hold him;
I do not know where this rogue is going, for he is surely the leader of cheats. "This talk is over—let it cease! Look ahead, O simple one! (111)
O friend, here is he, his face polished by the sweetness of his smile;
with the outstretched pillar of his arms, eager for the embrace of his beloved, this ocean of amorous play casts a bandhūka flower upon me. 112.

"Therefore arise, O bashful one; bind this rogue with your thick necklace of pearls, my friend, so that he does not go to Madhupurī. Thus spoke she, whose speech was rendered dull by the experience of love welling up within her.
Surely it does not fail to cause my friends' cries of lamentation to sprout again and again.
Alas, what misery! Out of childishness, I, with my wicked heart, repeatedly induced a knot of pride in my friend here, who was by nature so simple.

O teacher of the amorous arts of the throngs of gopīs, even though she was greedy for it, she did not obtain the intense thrill of your stainless pillar-like arms at that beginning, while you dwelt in the bower-houses fragrant with the lotuses of the Yamunā. 114. At the threshold... [of the bower].

When shall I again attend upon her as she rests upon your lap, her eyes closed in the bliss of sleep, her hair fragrant with the fresh scent of spring flowers, while I fan her with a cluster of young shoots?

I [behold] her, whose joy is sustained on the outskirts of Vṛndāvana; by the radiant splendor of the autumn night, the blossoming flowers of her braided hair have been withered, and the creeper-like vine of her arm is placed upon the slope of your shoulder.
When shall I laugh in secret, hidden in a bower with that lovely-faced one? Now, as I approach from afar to gather flowers,
you must pluck this sprout of *tulasī* on every bank along the river's edge.

"O Beloved of the Gopīs, when shall I, having learned of your whereabouts through some pretext, lead you to the bower at the proper time? Thus [ends] the account of Gokula at the lotus feet of the glorious Lord of Kaṃsa.
Having offered these individually, cultivate affection toward your attendants—
those whom the Lord, while carrying the companion of Kādambī upon his own lap as an ornament, favored with a heart deeply inclined toward love. 118.

O lover of the female swan, first joyfully inquire after the welfare of Vanamālā, whose graceful movements are ever-emerging; then offer these words of mine to the Enemy of Kaṃsa, who has long cherished her as his companion upon his chest.
"O virtuous one, have you forgotten this very eye?
Or rather, alas, do you remember, O connoisseur of flavor, how my friend’s limbs were overcome with anger at being rebuffed on the slopes of Mount Govardhana?"

If, with eyes bewildered by fear, he should here forcibly drag you away while seizing the Lord of Gokula—whose fresh peacock-feather crown is slipping—you should then joyfully address him with this seal of the Vedas: "O Makaradhvaja (God of Love), you who have been rendered powerless by the power of that Supreme Person, how can you, O wretch, now attempt to abduct the wife of that very one? You, whose heart was once pierced by the arrows of Cupid, have been made impotent by the glance of the Daughter of the Mountain; how then do you dare to act thus? Thus, having spoken these words, you should then depart quickly from that place. || 121 || *Note: This verse is part of Kṛṣṇamiśra’s *Prabodhacandrodaya*, Act IV.*
O friend, why this dullness in offering inquiries after your welfare?
For you, with a smile of delight, always perform the art of kissing even when merely touched by a sidelong glance from the mirror-like cheek of the Enemy of Mura.
Thinking that your dwelling, O Goddess, is within the creeper of my ear,
I, with a heart full of affection, go to you alone for refuge with great effort— secretly, even very secretly, into the hollow of the ear of the Vṛṣṇis while they are out of sight.
"O friend, tell Hari of Rādhā’s distress with a voice choked with sobs.
O best of birds, as you speak to the Kaustubha gem with humility, you should offer this petition out of love for an embrace from me."
O friend, how could such unfathomable forgetfulness have occurred even toward Rādhā? For how can affection for a fickle person bring about well-being?
[She who possesses] a flute, and the constant jingling of her girdle, bracelets, and anklets—

O jewel of the gods, will that intense abundance of the triple symphony— accompanied by the songs of throngs of wandering young women— once again manifest in person upon the sandy banks of the Yamunā, in the essence of Hari’s cosmic dance? 124
O Kamboja, you are a newcomer; you have no acquaintance with the supreme women of the cowherd community, nor do you possess even a scent of the weight of Rādhā’s virtues.
Nevertheless, I entreat you for the longing cherished within my heart.
For those of pure nature offer their affection even to the weary;
O friend, who gladdens the heart of the ocean, having taken Govinda with you, may you rejoice in comfort on the outskirts of Śrī Vṛndāvana.
"Or rather, how could your cow-pen be so dear to you? Ah, for it is the great majesty of the flute’s long-standing good fortune that triumphs therein!"—
having thus consoled her, who was overcome by an outpouring of love, in due course...
O brother, while Cāṇūra is being crushed,
you should relate before him a story concerning his retinue, which is playful with affection broken by anger, and which has manifested through ten incarnations. 127.
O great fish, my friend quickly cast the hook of her mind, baited with the lure of love, into the flood of my passion to catch you; but then,
having snapped that line called discernment, she was swallowed by you.
"Alas, alas! What can this wretched woman do?
Having seen the abundance of your amorous charms and your beautiful form, her mind, uplifted by supreme curiosity, has come into your presence. //128//
That you conceal your own limbs and yet manifest hardness—
is this not entirely appropriate for you in your tortoise form? O you who are ever devoted to Kaṃsa, even today your [hardness] still persists.
Clearly, a wave of intense love for her body, which has the form of a lap, arose;
for that Sairandhrī, who was fond of the paste of Malaya sandalwood, was embraced by you with supreme impetuosity as your own beloved. 130.
For a long time, the form consisting of Nara and Hari remained within you, and your activity never strayed from the path of remembrance;
yet here, in this supremely cruel deed, you have become like the humble Prahlāda.
O Vāmana, because you are excessively intent on piercing the hearts of others,
she— who, out of pride, disregarded her elders— joyfully imagined herself to be enriched by a kingdom of the mind through her affection for you. //131//
"This is indeed the fitting fruit for her: that she was cast far away by you, my dear friend, yet remained bound by the noose of affection.
O Lord, this cruel woman now longs to throw herself from Mount Bhṛgu."
O Lord of Bhṛgu, that which is harsh in this [matter] is appropriate for you;
yet this conduct of yours is difficult to comprehend, since even Nandīśvara himself, your direct preceptor, has fallen into oblivion regarding you.
The cows, long deprived of joy and harassed by swarms of demons, suddenly become like donkeys on the slopes of Govardhana, O ornament of the Raghus;
and the cowherd settlement falls into the state of being Virādha through your departure.
Now Mārīca clearly dances all around here;
this is a favorable time for you, O playful one, to rise up once more with your followers of donkeys.
Even now, we too are clearly innocent.

Spreading a luster upon your body like that of the autumnal sky, O Sīradhvaja, why do you not resort to this Vṛndāvana? O Omniscient One, you never harbor passion for anyone, yet you [do not honor] the Lord of Rati.
At times she feels hatred, at others she plots malice against those who seek her welfare;
though she dwells constantly absorbed in meditation and always delights in the teachings of the Sugata, alas, O compassionate-hearted one, you do not show her mercy! 136.

O Kalki, seated here, you take delight in the clever cowherds as they cut through the afflictions of the barbarians with the sweet, sword-blade-like tendril of their affectionate anger toward the swarms of intoxicated bees.
"You should send this message, further enhanced by the joy of the heroes,"—
having thus communicated all these words, whose phrasing was embraced by an outburst of love, with the region of your face moistened by tears from your eyes;
Then, O Lord of Birds, having sat for a moment near Govinda’s reply— which was like a drop of honey—
you beheld with your eyes the son of Nanda, who ought to be brought within the range of your vision.

O Lord of the flock of swans, do not harbor within yourself a sense of duality or conflict, thinking: "I am obedient to the gopīs who are honored throughout the world and intent on my welfare; yet this Mathurā, though clever, is reachable by me in three or four watches. (139)
How could it be appropriate for you, a man of merit, to associate with one in whom an unprecedented, pure luster shines within with joy, and by whom two waters, when mixed together,
can be instantly distinguished?
O Lord of the Kadamba groves, delay in the matter of union with Mathurā is not for you;
for one who is devoted to the Bhāgavatas, having attained love, always prevails as one who has turned away from the worldly pleasures of existence until the end of birth, being sweetened by devotion.
Victorious for a long time is a certain illustrious one, renowned as Śākara, who stands foremost among the wise upon this earth like the son of Vyāsa;
he is an abode of aesthetic sentiments (rasas) and remains unfamiliar with faults to those with sensitive hearts. //141//

May this composition, honored for its form as a dense arrangement of the playful pastimes of the Enemy of Mura, cause a thick wave of joy to sprout within the heart of that Lord, the Friend of the entire world and the Master of the Sarasvatīs. 142.
